chapter: Bands and bandleading in New Orleans
title: The steamer President job and his current band
summary: He quit the President's band, plays occasionally for the Captain, avoids high notes, and lists his current lineup with the Christians and Bill Voorhees and his view of how jazz should be played.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Yeah. You have down here about the steam of President.

Well I had played on the steam of President and I was going real good until I told the Captain I quit. So the night I quit I took another trumpet player on because just nothing wasn't coming out the horn. And Willie Gerbrecht said he'd give me a hand so I'd play a number and he'd play a number. But I let Willie play as much as he wanted to. And it was about five years before I contacted him. I've been playing off and on when the other band takes off. I played for the Captain about six times last year and a couple of times this year so far. But he likes the band. He would have got me back if I'd have been playing since I came back. But I don't try no real high notes anymore. I try to keep it like Bobby Hackett you know? And he's one of the world's best. And I don't try to go too high, overplay the horn. I think the public likes it a little bit better, Dick. The public doesn't always appreciate these gymnastics we do on a trumpet.

And I've been able to put the band across. I've been having a good man in my band. I might tell you my last lineup that I had when we played since Monk Hazel died I went with Emil Oyssen on drums. This is my latest band. I've been using Bobby Coquille on bass fiddle and I still have Bill Voorhees on piano. And my front line is Earl Christian, Emil Christian and myself. And they know my routine, they know my endings, the breaks. In fact Earl comes over here about every once a month and we just play together. Sometimes like Bill Voorhees wanted to come last night but Earl Christian had his horn out of Joe Grasavis getting fixed. But we like to present a real good jazz program and we're proud of the fact that we're from New Orleans. If anybody hears it, we wanted to hear it played the way we played it in the old days. And we're always trying to play it good. We never did try to think that we were too good at calling up a tune and calling it jazz. There are too many of the reading bands that do that. I'm talking to good reading bands. As soon as they go into a jazz tune, they call it up as if they're too good to play it right. And they play it willy as we used to say in the old days. But jazz music has to have a feeling to each note, a feeling to each beat, and it's got to be right. Well Dick, I enjoyed this conversation and you know I'm a man of few words.
